question: Consider the following \(100\) sets of \(10\) elements each: \[\begin{gathered} \{1,2,3,\ldots,10\},\\ \{11,12,13,\ldots,20\},\\ \{21,22,23,\ldots,30\},\\ \vdots\\ \{991,992,993,\ldots,1000\}. \end{gathered}\] How many of these sets contain exactly two multiples of \(7?\)
solution:
Each set contains either one or two multiples of \(7\), so counting all the multiples will determine how many sets contain two.

Every seven consecutive integers contain a multiple of \(7\), so each ten-number set contains at least one. Three multiples of \(7\) would have their smallest and largest at least \(14\) apart, whereas the endpoints of a ten-number set are only \(9\) apart. Thus no set contains three.

There are exactly \(142\) multiples of \(7\) from \(1\) through \(1000\), because
\[
7\cdot142=994\leq1000<1001=7\cdot143.
\]
Let \(t\) be the number of sets containing two multiples. The other \(100-t\) sets each contain one. Since the sets partition the integers from \(1\) through \(1000\), counting the multiples by set gives
\[
2t+(100-t)=142.
\]
Hence \(t=42\). The answer is \(\boxed{42}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Two multiples of \(7\) in the same set are \(7\) apart, so the earlier one must occupy one of the first three positions. This identifies the qualifying sets directly.

Each set starts with a number ending in \(1\). Its first three positions therefore contain numbers ending in \(1,2,3\). A multiple of \(7\) in any of these positions has its next multiple seven positions later, still inside the same set. Its preceding multiple lies outside the set.

Multiples of \(7\) ending in \(1,2,3\), respectively, have the forms
\[
21+70j,\qquad42+70j,\qquad63+70j,
\]
where \(j\) is a nonnegative integer. To see why the step is \(70\), note that two multiples with the same units digit differ by a multiple of both \(7\) and \(10\), hence by a multiple of \(70\).

For each of the three forms, \(j=0,1,\ldots,13\) gives a number at most \(1000\), while \(j=14\) exceeds \(1000\). Thus each form contributes \(14\) earlier multiples. Every qualifying set has exactly one such earlier multiple, so no set is missed or counted twice.

The total is \(3\cdot14=\boxed{42}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).
solutionMethods.label: Locate the earlier multiple
